subject: treehouse
reasoning:
I'm planning a single self-contained TypeScript module to build a stylized, low-poly treehouse using the SDK, favoring reliable primitives like b.part, b.sweep, and b.extrude for the trunk, branches, and structure while being cautious about API usage since I can't test it directly.

The overall scene is a tree with a treehouse perched on top, including a platform, ladder, roof, windows, rope bridge, lanterns, flag, and leaf clusters — rooted at ground level with the trunk sweeping upward with a slight lean and tapering radius, painted with a bark grain texture, scaled so the whole piece stands roughly 8 meters tall with the platform around 4.2m up.

I'm building the trunk as a proper skeletal chain so branches can attach to joints along it, then sweeping branch geometry off those joints using bezier curves with tapered capsule radii and bark-matching color. For attaching smaller details like branches, I'm using a surface-based placement system that lets me position elements around the trunk's circumference at specific angles and elevations.

Next I'm sketching out the platform structure — a wooden deck plank, supporting cylindrical posts beneath it, and the walls of a small treehouse box sitting above the deck with its own wall color.

For the actual roof slopes, I'm thinking simpler: use two tilted box slabs rotated around the z-axis for the sloped sides instead of extruding a gable shape.

Recalculating wall and roof heights to figure out ridge position and slope angle from the deck top to the peak.

For each slab, I'm computing slab length including overhang, centering it at the midpoint between eave and ridge, and working out the rotation needed about the Z axis so the raised end points toward the ridge—left slab gets positive rotation, right slab negative, keeping the outer edges flush with the wall width.

Now I'm working out the gable triangles that fill the top of the front and back walls under the roof peak: a flat extruded triangle spanning the wall width at the eave height, rising to the ridge height, thin in depth and centered on the front/back wall plane.

For the roof slabs, I'm positioning them just above the walls at the correct pitch angle so their undersides meet the gable triangle edges cleanly.

Then I'm placing window elements on the front wall: a warm glowing glass pane, a darker frame box behind it, and shutters flanking each side.

I also need a door on the front face offset from center, a second window on the left, and a ladder made of two rails leaning from the ground up to the deck edge near the trunk base.

Writing rung loop logic...

Now thinking through the trunk shape: a tapered catmull-rom sweep from the ground up into the deck, radius shrinking from 0.5 near the base to 0.28 higher up, with a slight curve for naturalism. I need to watch out for the round end caps extending past the path's start/end points, since that could make the trunk dip below the floor or poke oddly into the deck, so I'm adjusting where the path starts to compensate.

I'm setting up the trunk chain with the spine role and letting its first joint stand in as the single root joint of the skeleton, since a chain's first joint without a parent qualifies as root per the requirements.

For the canopy, I'm thinking through using low-poly icosahedron blobs as leaf clusters in varied greens, clustering them near the top around y~5.5-6.5 so they surround the house roof without fully blocking it.

For the ground, I'm adding a grass patch disc beneath the scene, checking that the cylinder's placement doesn't sink more than the 2% tolerance into the floor—settling on a thinner height centered slightly below zero to stay within that margin.

Skipping a rope bridge idea since there's no second trunk to anchor it to. Instead I'm planning railings around the platform using posts and rods along the deck edges, leaving a gap near the front for a ladder entry point.

Placing the ladder near the front-left corner of the deck, slightly leaning against the trunk, with rails running from near ground level up to the deck height and rungs spaced evenly between them.

I need to account for the house walls at x±1.5, z±1.3, leaving a shallow 0.3-deep deck strip at the front. The front railing needs a gap for the ladder near x=-1.2, so I'm splitting the front rail segment to leave room there.

I'm placing corner posts and rail rods along the deck edges, sizing cylinders for posts and rods so they align with the deck height and connect properly at the corners, then considering support pillars beneath the deck.

Still planning the branch geometry...

Now for the canopy I'm sweeping several branches upward from the trunk top into the foliage area, then building the leaf clusters as jittered icosahedron blobs using a seeded random generator for natural variation.

For texturing I'm applying bark grain along the trunk sweep and mottled green patterns across the leaf clusters, then setting up the imports needed from the builder library plus THREE itself, and adding a small flag detail at the top.

Adding pole, flag, and lanterns...

I'll skip the rope bridge and ladder details to keep things simpler, and most other parts can just attach to the nearest existing joint since the whole structure is static anyway.

For the actual build, I'm using icosahedron geometry with flat shading for faceted canopy blobs, rotation options for angled roof pieces, and extruded outlines for the gable walls.

Now I'm checking that the gable apex height roughly matches where the roof slabs meet at the ridge, and positioning the front and back gables symmetrically at z=±1.3 using a loop. I'm sizing the roof slab boxes to span the full depth of the building, around 3.1 units in z with 2.0 length and 0.12 thickness.

Verifying the left roof slab's rotated position so its upper edge aligns near x=0 at the ridge and its outer end sits just past the wall top for proper eave overhang. Then I'm setting up the deck as a wide flat box below the walls, sizing the walls themselves around 3.0 by 2.0 by 2.6, and starting on the railing position near the deck's front edge.

Now I'm placing the front-wall details: a door box positioned left of center with its bottom flush to the deck, a window frame to the right with a glowing glass panel behind it, and thin cross-bar strips layered in front to give the window divided panes.

For the other walls, I'm planning a reusable window helper that handles both front/back orientation and side walls by swapping box dimensions depending on which face it's mounted on, so I can place matching windows symmetrically without duplicating code.

Simplifying with a helper function to compute dimensions per axis...

Still working out the axis-dependent dimension mapping...

I'm setting up an offset helper to position frame elements relative to the wall face depending on which axis they're mounted on, plus noting details like the window glow color and deciding to skip extra hanging rope details for simplicity.

Now I'm mapping out canopy foliage positions as overlapping colored blobs clustered above the trunk, varying their coordinates, radii, and green shades to build a layered, natural-looking tree canopy.

Now I'm working out the branch geometry, sweeping bezier curves from the trunk outward with tapering radii and attaching them to bone joints along the trunk's skeletal chain so they follow its curvature naturally. Adding the flagpole, placing its base inside the roof ridge so it reads as mounted rather than floating.

Placing lanterns flanking the door symmetrically at roughly x ±0.4, near y 4.85-5.0, since door is centered at x=0.

For fun I'll add a tire swing hanging from a branch tip, using thin rods down to a torus seat positioned and rotated flat to look like a tire.

Adjusting the ground plane position slightly and repositioning the decorative stones so they sit properly on the surface rather than floating. Now I'm starting to lay out the actual module code, setting up the builder with a trunk chain defined by a catmull-rom curve.

I'm deciding on material and color choices for the tree—bark with a grain pattern, mottled leaf colors on faceted icosahedrons—and sketching out the deck and wall color palette using warm wood tones.

Now I'm thinking through the roof, gable, and window colors, wondering whether to use the rng helper for slight jitter in leaf placement or skip it to keep things deterministic and avoid API uncertainty.

Defining color palette constants...

Adding tree branches...

For the gable end, I'm extruding a triangular outline with the apex rising above the wall top, making sure the outline points sit correctly on the wall face and the thickness is centered at the right depth for both gable ends.

Setting up pane positioning logic...

For the ladder, I'm positioning two angled rail rods from ground to roof height with a tilt matching the trunk curve, then generating ten evenly spaced rungs connecting them using wood-colored rods.

I'm also noticing some near-duplicate posts between the deck's support posts and the rail posts at similar coordinates — I'll just move the support posts inward to around (±1.2, ±1.2) so they sit clear of the trunk and don't overlap the rail posts, while still leaving clearance for the ladder footprint near x=-0.7 to -1.1, z=1.2 to 1.6.

Now I'm shifting focus to the tire swing — placing support rods running from a branch point near the canopy down to the top of a torus-shaped tire hanging below.

The tire swing sits just outside the deck's left edge, so it clears fine. For stones, I'm placing two flat dodecahedrons of different sizes at scattered positions, and then I'm setting up a cylinder for the grass disc base.

Now I'm adding the flagpole with a trim-colored rod and a small flag box offset to one side at the top, then defining mottled leaf-color blends for the canopy and placing several foliage blobs around the tree's upper structure at varying positions and sizes.
